challenges.name: Apple (the Apple dance)
challenges.originator: Kelley Heyer
challenges.originator_story: Kelley Heyer, a NYC-based actor and TikTok creator, posted the 'Apple' dance on 14-15 June 2024, calling it Brat's most underappreciated song. It became a defining 'Brat summer' trend; Charli XCX brought Heyer onstage during the SWEAT tour ('She made the fucking dance, bitch'). Heyer filed a choreography copyright application (30 Aug 2024) and licensed the dance to Fortnite ('Bratty' emote, Dec 2024) and Netflix.
challenges.timeline: 14-15 June 2024 dance -> summer 2024 virality (tied to 'Brat summer') -> Aug 2024 Roblox/copyright friction -> Dec 2024 Fortnite deal -> April 2025 Roblox lawsuit -> 2025 settlement.
challenges.fun_facts: Modern choreography-IP test case: Heyer sued Roblox (filed 11 April 2025) alleging it earned ~$123,000 selling the dance as an emote (Aug-Nov 2024) without a signed deal; Roblox said it had agreed to license for $9,000. Amicably resolved 2025. NOTE: the genuinely viral 'Brat' dance is Apple, not 'Von Dutch.'

challenges.name: Renegade
challenges.originator: Jalaiah Harmon
challenges.originator_story: Jalaiah Harmon, a formally trained dancer from Fayetteville, Georgia, choreographed the Renegade in her bedroom at age 14 on Sept 25, 2019, and first posted it on Funimate and Instagram. The dance exploded on TikTok via other accounts (notably @global.jones) and made stars of white creators like Charli D'Amelio and Addison Rae, while Harmon went almost entirely uncredited. She became the central example of Black girls' viral choreography being lifted without attribution, until a Feb 13, 2020 New York Times profile by Taylor Lorenz, 'The Original Renegade,' established her authorship.
challenges.timeline: Choreographed and posted on Funimate/Instagram Sept 25 2019 -> reposted and spread on TikTok Oct 2019, popularized by Charli D'Amelio and Addison Rae without crediting Harmon -> peak virality Dec 2019-Feb 2020 -> NYT profile (Taylor Lorenz) Feb 13 2020 restores credit -> K Camp publicly thanks her, she performs at NBA All-Star Game Feb 16 2020.
challenges.fun_facts: Canonical case of an uncredited Black teen creator. Harmon developed the routine partly from a friend (Kaliyah Davis) collaboration and built it from existing moves (the Woah, the Wave). Sparked the broader 'who owns a viral dance' / credit-for-Black-creators conversation; she later got a Togethxr docuseries ('I Am: Jalaiah') and a Sufjan Stevens music video cameo.

Brown built the track from a borrowed lap steel guitar plus spoons, tambourine, and beatboxing, and dedicated it to his grandmother's mantra ('Get up. Go do something productive'). challenges.name: The Original Harlem Shake (the real dance, 1981)
challenges.song: (no single song — street dance performed at Rucker Park, Harlem)
challenges.originator: Albert Leopold 'Al B.' Boyce — uncredited Black creator
challenges.originator_story: Albert Leopold 'Al B.' Boyce (also known as Ali Saadat / Al Cisco) created the original Harlem Shake in 1981, first called 'The Albee' after him; he performed it during breaks at the Entertainer's Basketball Classic at Rucker Park. challenges.timeline: 1981 Rucker Park creation -> popularized by Crazy Boyz crew -> G. Dep 'Let's Get It' (2001) video mainstream -> Bow Wow and Jadakiss videos -> 2006 'Chicken Noodle Soup' revival.
challenges.fun_facts: Al B. died in 2006 without profiting — a textbook case of an uncredited Black creator. Some sources cite Ethiopian Eskista as an influence.

challenges.originator: Lupino Lane (stage originator); Adele England (participation-dance elaborator)
challenges.originator_story: Lupino Lane popularized the jaunty Cockney strut in the 1937 musical Me and My Girl. Dance-hall instructor Adele England (Locarno Dance Halls) elaborated it into a participation dance after C.L. Heimann commissioned her to turn the walk into a full routine.
challenges.timeline: 1937 stage (opened Dec 1937, Victoria Palace) -> 1938 international craze. The Times Oct 1938: 'While dictators rage and statesmen talk, all Europe dances to The Lambeth Walk.'
challenges.fun_facts: SA Mann denounced it Jan 1939 as 'Jewish mischief and animalistic hopping.' In 1942 Charles Ridley made a propaganda film editing Nazi goose-stepping to the tune.

challenges.name: Lindy Hop
challenges.originator: 'Shorty George' Snowden (named it); Frankie Manning (first aerial) — Harlem Savoy Ballroom
challenges.originator_story: Harlem vernacular jazz dance (late 1920s-30s, Savoy Ballroom). 'Shorty George' Snowden is credited with naming the dance (after Lindbergh's flight); Frankie Manning pioneered the first aerial/air step (1935) and became its global ambassador, winning a 1989 Tony for choreographing Black and Blue.
challenges.timeline: Snowden reinvents the breakaway 1928 -> Manning's first aerial 1935 -> 1930s-40s peak -> revived from the 1980s.
challenges.fun_facts: Other founders: Herbert 'Whitey' White, Norma Miller, 'Twistmouth George' Ganaway. A Black American vernacular jazz dance.

challenges.name: The Charleston
challenges.originator: Song by James P. Johnson (1923); dance from Gullah/Geechie traditions
challenges.originator_story: The song 'The Charleston' was written by Black composer/pianist James P. Johnson (lyrics by Cecil Mack) for the 1923 all-Black Broadway show Runnin' Wild. The dance derives from Gullah/Geechie traditions Johnson saw among South Carolina dockworkers, with roots in the African-derived Juba dance. Popularized to white audiences by Josephine Baker and others.
challenges.timeline: Gullah/Geechie roots -> Runnin' Wild (Oct 1923) -> 1920s craze; Baker takes it to Paris 1925.
challenges.fun_facts: A documented case of Black folk origins commercialized for white audiences.

challenges.name: The Black Bottom
challenges.song: The Black Bottom (from George White's Scandals, 1926; also Alberta Hunter and various)
challenges.originator: Emerged among African Americans (rural South, c.1907); Alberta Hunter/Perry Bradford/Billy Pierce contested as originators; mainstreamed by white performers
challenges.originator_story: The Black Bottom emerged among African Americans in the rural South (documented as early as 1907, with New Orleans roots), derived from 'the Echo.' Blues singer Alberta Hunter claimed to have introduced it c.1925; songwriter Perry Bradford published 'Original Black Bottom Dance' (1919/1926); choreographer Billy Pierce is credited on some sheet music. It was mainstreamed — and arguably appropriated — by white performer Ann Pennington in George White's Scandals of 1926. A documented pattern of Black originators eclipsed by white Broadway popularizers.
challenges.timeline: c.1907 rural South emergence -> 1919-26 Northern migration -> Ann Pennington's Scandals of 1926 -> overtook the Charleston as No. 1 social dance.
challenges.fun_facts: Documented appropriation of a Black folk dance by white Broadway performers.

challenges.name: Blinding Lights
challenges.originator: Adam Snyder, Nate Nale and Greg Dahl (for the routine popularized via The Tonight Show)
challenges.originator_story: The Weeknd's 'Blinding Lights' spawned one of the largest dance challenges of 2020. The specific routine that Addison Rae performed on The Tonight Show in March 2021 was credited by NBC to Adam Snyder, Nate Nale and Greg Dahl, who were later invited onto the show. Because 'Blinding Lights' generated multiple distinct viral routines worldwide, attribution of 'the' Blinding Lights dance is genuinely contested.
challenges.timeline: The Weeknd releases 'Blinding Lights' Nov 2019 -> multiple dance challenges spread through 2020 (often family/quarantine versions) -> the routine Rae performed is credited to Snyder, Nale and Dahl, who appear on The Tonight Show Apr 5 2021. (Origin date and original-video URL unconfirmed; needs dedicated research to separate the competing routines.)
challenges.fun_facts: 'Blinding Lights' became the longest-charting song in Billboard Hot 100 history, and its dance challenges were correspondingly sprawling. Caution: unlike single-author dances such as Renegade, there is no one undisputed 'Blinding Lights dance' originator; the names here are specifically the creators NBC credited for the Tonight Show routine.

challenges.name: The Woah
challenges.song: (used across many songs; no single song)
challenges.originator: DISPUTED — Young Deji vs 10k Cash vs DJ Dangerous vs TisaKorean (Houston/Dallas)
challenges.originator_story: Genuinely contested origin, primarily from Houston/Dallas Texas (NOT Milwaukee). Young Deji (Houston; Taylor Gang) claims he invented it; 10k Cash, TisaKorean and DJ Dangerous are also linked; DJ Dangerous posted 'receipts' arguing Young Deji conflated an earlier dance ('The Dejo') with The Woah. The FADER: 'The truth about who created The Woah is now murky and confusing.'
challenges.timeline: ~2018 emerges in Texas -> adopted by Lil Uzi Vert, Drake, Travis Scott (SNL 6 Oct 2018, criticized for not crediting the kids) -> ubiquitous 2018-2020.
challenges.fun_facts: The original brief's 'Milwaukee/KTumbla/414BigFrank' framing is NOT supported by available sources, which point to Texas — flagged as conflicting/unverified.
